text: Congressman, thank you for being here with us. Yeah, there we go. That's the spirit. I'm here for it. Well, Congressman Torres, you. You've distinguished yourself as a pro crypto Democrat. You're very out front on the issue. You recently established the Congressional Crypto Congress with your crypto caucus with your colleague on the other side of the aisle, Congressman Tom Emmer. But you also come from, I think, the poorest district in the country. So why do you care about crypto? Help tie these sort of issues together for me?

text: Well, it's an honor to be here. I mean, I see crypto as a profoundly progressive technology. It has the power to revolutionize the Internet by creating a new layer known as Web3, and it has the power to revolutionize finance. And as you said, I represent the lowest income congressional district in America. I represent people who have been left behind by the traditional financial system. 20% of the Bronx is unbanked, 30% is underbanked. There are immigrants in my district who pay exorbitant fees simply to transfer their remittances to loved ones abroad. And so I'm drawn to the power of blockchain to create a better and cheaper, faster payment system. You know, about a decade ago, the Department of Consumer affairs did a study and found that the lowest income people spend more than $200 million on check cashing fees here in New York. Right. These are people who are preyed upon by predatory financial services. And so I feel like blockchain has the power to enable real time transactions. Stablecoin has the power to digitize the dollar. And the combination of those two technologies, the ability to move the dollar at the speed of the blockchain, can create a better and cheaper and faster payment system that could liberate the lowest income from the high fees and long delays of the traditional financial system. So that, to me, is one of the greatest appeals that crypto has.

text: Look, I think any party or any country or any civilization that declares war on its own tech sector will ultimately rot from within. I mean, I see technology as the greatest strategic asset not only for the United States, but for humanity. For most of human history, there was practically no economic growth. You know, my understanding is from classical Greece to the Reformation, the economy grew by 2% a century. And then after the Reformation, after the advent of the printing press, it grew by 20% a century. And then after the Industrial Revolution, particularly in the 20th century, it grew by 2,000% a century. And so the clear lesson of history is that technology is the single greatest catalyst for human progress and prosperity. And every party in America should be pro technology, like emerging technologies like blockchain and biotech and AI and quantum computing should be neither Democratic nor Republican. It should be something that all of us embrace as a catalyst for human progress. So that's the mindset that we should internalize within the Democratic Party. But I feel like the central divide is not between Democrat and Republicans. It's not so much ideological as it is generational. I do feel like there's a new guard of Democrats who are much more open to embracing emerging technologies like blockchain. But as you know, Congress remains a gerontocracy. text: So the, the social media virality is a byproduct rather than the purpose. You know, when I'm crafting questions for hearing, when I'm preparing to cross examine, you know, like the. For, you know, someone like Gary Gensler, the goal is not to go viral. I actually feel like if you try to go viral, it will fail almost all the time. The goal is to take a complicated issue and distill it to its essence, to get to the core of an issue. And that's what I. I did not realize I would go viral. But, you know, when I brought up the Pokemon hypothetical. It was not meant to be performative. It was actually meant to expose the flaws in Gary Gensler's theory of investment contracts. Because I said to Gary, look, if I were to sell you a Pokemon card, am I engaged in an unregistered securities offering? And he said, no. And then I said, what if I were to engage in the same transaction through a blockchain? Is that a security offering? And then he said, it depends. And I said, why should it depend if you're technology neutral? Like, why should the nature of the technology you use magically transform a commodity into a security? And I did not realize that that highly technical conversation about investment contracts would go viral. But my goal is not to be viral. My goal is to penetrate to the core of an issue. I did the same with the Yankee tickets. I said to Gensler, you know, purchasing a Yankee ticket to access a Yankee game is no different from purchasing stoner cats NFT to access an animated web series. And if you were to adopt the Gensler theory of investment contracts and say that anything that appreciates in value or anything that could be resold in a secondary market is a security, that would transform almost everything into a security. Collectibles would become a security. Artwork would become a security. And so I think my point was to show that his theory of investment contracts was so open ended that it invites the weaponization of government against the crypto industry.
